addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- code-simplifier:code-simplifier: Simplifies and refines code for clarity, consistency, and maintainability while preserving all functionality. Focuses on recently modified code unless instructed otherwise. (Tools: All tools)

- docs-consistency-guard: Documentation agent that audits docs for staleness and inconsistency AND generates/updates documentation on request. Use proactively when reviewing any PR that touches CLAUDE.md, docs/adr/, CONTRIBUTING.md, or docs/architecture.md. Also invoke when the user asks "is the documentation up to date?", "update the milestone", "scaffold the ADR for X", "add this to the ADR index", "add a TODO item", "scaffold a README for X", or "create a doc stub for Y." (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash, Write, Edit)

- driver-boundary-guard: Specialized reviewer for values that cross a DRIVER boundary — anything DataQ receives from a database connector, pyiceberg, pandas/pyarrow, or a cloud SDK and then type-narrows (isinstance / dtype checks / hasattr). Audits whether the covering tests hand-build the value in the shape our model expects (the "fixture encodes our model" defect that hid (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- entire-search: Search Entire checkpoint history and transcripts with `entire search --json`. Use proactively when the user asks about previous work, commits, sessions, prompts, or historical context in this repository. (Tools: Bash)

- Explore: Fast read-only search agent for locating code. Use it to find files by pattern (eg. "src/components/**/*.tsx"), grep for symbols or keywords (eg. "API endpoints"), or answer "where is X defined / which files reference Y." Do NOT use it for code review, design-doc auditing, cross-file consistency checks, or open-ended analysis — it reads excerpts rather than whole files and will miss content past its read window. When calling, specify search breadth: "quick" for a single targeted lookup, "medium" for moderate exploration, or "very thorough" to search across multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- migration-safety: Specialized reviewer for Alembic migrations under backend/alembic/versions/. Audits for backward-incompatible operations that would break running code during a deploy, per working-agreement (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- orchestration-abstraction-guard: Specialized reviewer that audits backend code for provider-specific branching that bypasses the OrchestrationProvider abstraction. Use this proactively when reviewing any PR that touches backend/app/orchestration/, backend/app/services/, or backend/app/api/ — especially any code path handling ADF or Airflow events, trigger bindings, or pipeline_runs. Also invoke when the user asks "does this go through the abstraction?" or similar. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- pr-review-toolkit:code-reviewer: Use this agent when you need to review code for adherence to project guidelines, style guides, and best practices. This agent should be used proactively after writing or modifying code, especially before committing changes or creating pull requests. It will check for style violations, potential issues, and ensure code follows the established patterns in CLAUDE.md. Also the agent needs to know which files to focus on for the review. In most cases this will be recently completed work which is unstaged in git (can be retrieved by running git diff). However there can be cases where this is different, make sure to specify this as the agent input when calling the agent. Typical triggers include the user asking for a review of a feature they just implemented, the assistant proactively reviewing its own newly-written code before declaring a task done, and a final pre-PR check before opening a pull request. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:code-simplifier: Use this agent when code has been written or modified and needs to be simplified for clarity, consistency, and maintainability while preserving all functionality. This agent should be triggered automatically after completing a coding task or writing a logical chunk of code. It simplifies code by following project best practices while retaining all functionality. The agent focuses only on recently modified code unless instructed otherwise.

Examples:

<example>
Context: The assistant has just implemented a new feature that adds user authentication to an API endpoint.
user: "Please add authentication to the /api/users endpoint"
assistant: "I've implemented the authentication for the /api/users endpoint. Here's the code:"
<function call omitted for brevity>
<commentary>
Since a logical chunk of code has been written (authentication feature), use the Task tool to launch the code-simplifier agent to improve the code's clarity and maintainability while preserving functionality.
</commentary>
assistant: "Now let me use the code-simplifier agent to refine this implementation for better clarity and maintainability"
</example>

<example>
Context: The assistant has just fixed a bug by adding several conditional checks.
user: "Fix the null pointer exception in the data processor"
assistant: "I've added the necessary null checks to prevent the exception:"
<function call omitted for brevity>
<commentary>
After modifying code to fix a bug, use the code-simplifier agent to ensure the fix follows best practices and maintains code quality.
</commentary>
assistant: "Let me refine this bug fix using the code-simplifier agent to ensure it follows our best practices"
</example>

<example>
Context: The assistant has just refactored a function to improve performance.
user: "Optimize the data sorting algorithm for better performance"
assistant: "I've optimized the sorting algorithm. Here's the updated implementation:"
<function call omitted for brevity>
<commentary>
After completing a performance optimization task, use the code-simplifier agent to ensure the optimized code is also clear and maintainable.
</commentary>
assistant: "Now I'll use the code-simplifier agent to ensure the optimized code is also clear and follows our coding standards"
</example> (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:comment-analyzer: Use this agent when you need to analyze code comments for accuracy, completeness, and long-term maintainability. This includes (1) after generating large documentation comments or docstrings, (2) before finalizing a pull request that adds or modifies comments, (3) when reviewing existing comments for potential technical debt or comment rot, and (4) when you need to verify that comments accurately reflect the code they describe. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:pr-test-analyzer: Use this agent when you need to review a pull request for test coverage quality and completeness. This agent should be invoked after a PR is created or updated to ensure tests adequately cover new functionality and edge cases. Typical triggers include the user asking whether tests on a freshly-created PR are thorough, an updated PR adding new logic that needs coverage analysis, and a final pre-merge double-check before marking a PR ready. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:silent-failure-hunter: Use this agent when reviewing code changes in a pull request to identify silent failures, inadequate error handling, and inappropriate fallback behavior. This agent should be invoked proactively after completing a logical chunk of work that involves error handling, catch blocks, fallback logic, or any code that could potentially suppress errors. Examples:

<example>
Context: Daisy has just finished implementing a new feature that fetches data from an API with fallback behavior.
Daisy: "I've added error handling to the API client. Can you review it?"
Assistant: "Let me use the silent-failure-hunter agent to thoroughly examine the error handling in your changes."
<Task tool invocation to launch silent-failure-hunter agent>
</example>

<example>
Context: Daisy has created a PR with changes that include try-catch blocks.
Daisy: "Please review PR #1234"
Assistant: "I'll use the silent-failure-hunter agent to check for any silent failures or inadequate error handling in this PR."
<Task tool invocation to launch silent-failure-hunter agent>
</example>

<example>
Context: Daisy has just refactored error handling code.
Daisy: "I've updated the error handling in the authentication module"
Assistant: "Let me proactively use the silent-failure-hunter agent to ensure the error handling changes don't introduce silent failures."
<Task tool invocation to launch silent-failure-hunter agent>
</example> (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:type-design-analyzer: Use this agent when you need expert analysis of type design in your codebase. Specifically use it (1) when introducing a new type to ensure it follows best practices for encapsulation and invariant expression, (2) during pull request creation to review all types being added, and (3) when refactoring existing types to improve their design quality. The agent will provide both qualitative feedback and quantitative ratings on encapsulation, invariant expression, usefulness, and enforcement. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- qa-verifier: QA/QE agent that (1) runs the full local verification battery mirroring CI's required checks before any commit/push/PR, (2) audits test quality on changed code — failure-mode coverage, mocked-seam smells, coverage on changed files (Week-8 ≥80% gate), and (3) exercises the running application with data-level scenarios — authoring suites/checks through the real API, negative and edge-case inputs, authz probes — against the local stack's seeded demo data. Use proactively before pushing a branch or opening a PR, after writing or modifying tests, or when the user asks "run the gate", "is this ready to push?", "is this tested enough?", or "smoke the app with bad data". (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- regression-mutation-verifier: Proves that a new regression test actually fails against the unfixed code. Reverts the fix inside a throwaway git worktree, runs only the new test, and reports whether it fails for the RIGHT reason — catching tests that pass no matter what (the (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash, Edit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

- ui-tester: End-to-end UI QA agent that exercises DataQ's frontend on BOTH desktop and mobile viewports (functionality + rendering) against the running app, AND audits backend↔frontend feature parity — flagging backend capabilities with no frontend surface (and frontend calls with no backend). Use when the user asks to "test the UI", "check mobile rendering", "find backend/frontend gaps", "is this feature wired end-to-end", or before a release. Drives a live browser via the Playwright MCP and reads code for the parity audit. (Tools: All tools)

## claude.ai Microsoft Learn
# Microsoft Learn MCP Server

This server gives structured access to official Microsoft and Azure documentation via three tools:

## Tools

### microsoft_docs_search
Search official documentation and return up to 10 concise, high-quality content chunks (max 500 tokens each), including title, URL, and excerpt.

- Use first to get a quick, reliable overview
- Ideal for grounding answers in Microsoft knowledge

### microsoft_code_sample_search
Search for code snippets and examples in official Microsoft Learn documentation and return up to 20 relevant, high-quality code samples.

- Use when you need to provide sample Microsoft/Azure related code in your answers.  
- Ideal for generating code snippets or practical implementation examples.  
- Optional parameter `language` can filter results. 

### microsoft_docs_fetch
Fetch and convert full Microsoft documentation pages to markdown.

- Use after search when you need full content from a specific URL
- Required for detailed tutorials, troubleshooting, prerequisites, code samples, or when search results are incomplete or outdated

## Workflow

1. Use `microsoft_docs_search` to find relevant documents.
2. If you need code examples or practical snippets, use `microsoft_code_sample_search`.
3. If deeper or complete information is needed, use `microsoft_docs_fetch`.

**Search gives breadth. Code Sample Search gives practical examples. Fetch gives depth.**

All content comes from Microsoft Learn or official sources, returned in clean markdown format.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.

{"body":"## Problem

On the Results view's **Pipeline runs** tab, the "Failure reason" column (`frontend/src/pages/Results.tsx`, the `columns: ColumnsType<PipelineRun>` array around the `failure_reason` entry) has no `width` and no `ellipsis`. `pipeline_runs.failure_reason` is `String(2048)` on the backend (`backend/app/db/models.py`) — a real provider error string (ADF/Airflow) can be very long. With no bound, a long value stretches the whole column (and the table's horizontal scrollbar with it) to fit the entire string on one line, making the scrollbar unusably long and the table hard to use.

## Fix

Give the column a bounded fixed width with single-line ellipsis, and reveal the full text on hover — the standard antd pattern: `width: <px>` + `ellipsis: { showTitle: false }` on the column, with the cell's `render` wrapped in a `<Tooltip title={fullText}>` (custom tooltip since `showTitle: false` suppresses antd's own native-title one). Keep the existing `'—'` null placeholder un-tooltipped.

## Scope

1. Primary: the pipeline-runs "Failure reason" column.
2. Audit every other antd `Table` (`ColumnsType` definitions) across `frontend/src` for columns rendering unbounded free text (error/reason/message/description-like content) and apply the same treatment where warranted. Columns that are already bounded (tags, timestamps, fixed-vocabulary status, names capped at input) are out of scope.","comments":[{"id":"IC_kwDOSBITx88AAAABN2yAJw","author":{"login":"TheurgicDuke771"},"authorAssociation":"OWNER","body":"Audit result (full detail in PR #1185's description, "Audit — tables inspected"): the only other candidate for this bug class found across every `ColumnsType` table in `frontend/src` was `RunDetail.tsx`'s "Observed" column (`observed_value`, rendered via `ScalarValue`/`formatScalar`, which can `JSON.stringify` an object).

Determination: **verified-benign, scoped out of this fix.** Traced the GX translation path (`backend/app/datasources/gx_runner.py`, `monitors.py`) — for every check kind DataQ ships (expectation aggregates, freshness/volume/anomaly/comparison), `observed_value` is a compact scalar/small dict (counts, percentages, a timestamp); the actual unexpected-value lists live in `sample_failures`/`partial_unexpected_list`, which this column doesn't render. JSON output also has natural wrap points (commas/brackets), unlike the single unbroken provider-error string that caused this issue. It's also the row's primary "answer," so truncating it behind a hover is a worse tradeoff than for a secondary "reason" column.

No follow-up issue filed — recording the determination here per the fixed-or-filed rule so it isn't dropped silently. If a real-world `observed_value` payload is ever found to actually stretch the table, re-open or file fresh against that evidence.","createdAt":"2026-08-08T05:57:57Z","includesCreatedEdit":false,"isMinimized":false,"minimizedReason":"","reactionGroups":[],"url":"https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1184#issuecomment-5224824871","viewerDidAuthor":true},{"id":"IC_kwDOSBITx88AAAABN4he8A","author":{"login":"TheurgicDuke771"},"authorAssociation":"OWNER","body":"**Correction to the "verified-benign" determination above.**

A live user report against the run-detail page's Observed column contradicted the "always a compact scalar/small dict" premise, so it was re-investigated (#1207).

The premise holds for `anomaly` and for GX/custom-SQL expectations (incl. #1201's UC custom-SQL fix) — both genuinely store a fixed small scalar shape in `observed_value`. It does **not** hold for `schema_drift` (`added`/`removed` column-name lists + a `type_changed` list, one entry per drifted column) or `comparison` (ADR 0015 — `per_column`/`column_mismatch_counts` dicts keyed by every compared column). Both scale with column count, not a fixed shape, and the original audit (tracing `gx_runner.py`/`monitors.py`) didn't reach the two monitor-kind services (`schema_drift.py`, `comparison_run.py`) that build `observed_value` themselves outside the shared GX runner.

Fixed in #1207 (bounded width + tooltip on the Observed column, same pattern as this issue's fix). Recording the correction here per the working agreement — determinations get corrected on the record, never silently.

31	   `dataq-app-kv-aw6laj` secrets by name (values piped directly between `az`
32	   and OpenBao's HTTP API, never printed or written to disk), verified the
33	   name sets are now identical.

35	   `connections` / `suites` / `checks`** — nuked the local schema, re-ran
36	   migrations, opened a **temporary** Postgres firewall rule, copied the four
37	   tables straight from prod via `psycopg2`, closed the firewall rule
38	   immediately after. 13 connections, 12 suites, 30 checks, 8 users.

45	   /assets` was empty. Fixed by re-`PATCH`ing each suite with its own

47	   changing anything else. 10 assets now exist, correctly deduplicated.

49	   connections carried prod's *incremental* lineage watermark
50	   (`2026-07-27`) into a local DB whose `lineage_edges` table was never
51	   copied. Left alone, a future local warehouse-lineage refresh would have
52	   silently started from that stale cursor and permanently skipped
53	   everything before it. Reset `lineage_watermark` /
54	   `lineage_last_refresh_at` / `lineage_last_tier` to `NULL` on both UC
55	   connections.

59	suites won't auto-fire on a cron or an orchestration trigger. Lineage edges
60	themselves were not copied and are not backfilled (they only populate via a
61	live refresh, which is off locally by default — same as prod).
62	
63	---
64	
65	## 2. Replication runbook (redo this from scratch)
66	
67	Run this in `~/Coding/Python/DataQ` unless noted. Requires `az` logged in
68	with Key Vault read + Container App secret read + the shared Postgres
69	server's firewall-rule permissions (deployer/`dataq-admin`-tier access).
70	
71	### 2.1 Bring up both stacks
72	
73	```bash
74	cd ~/Coding/Python/DataQ
75	docker compose up -d                       # postgres/redis/openbao/mailpit/api/worker/frontend
76	
77	cd ~/Coding/Python/DataQ-harness/local
78	./harness_local.sh up                      # requires DataQ's stack up first (joins dataq_default)
79	```
80	
81	### 2.2 Multi-user OTP sign-in
82	
83	`.env`'s `DATAQ_SIGNIN_EMAIL` **is** the allowlist — `docker-compose.yml`
84	wires it straight into `AUTH_OTP_ALLOWED_EMAILS` verbatim
85	(`${DATAQ_SIGNIN_EMAIL?...}`, not a separate override). Comma-separate it for
86	multiple users:
87	
88	```bash
89	# .env is deliberately unwritable by the Edit tool in an AI session (secrets
90	# guard) — append with a shell redirect instead:
91	printf 'DATAQ_SIGNIN_EMAIL=you@example.com,teammate@example.com\n' >> .env
92	docker compose up -d api worker             # env is a start-time snapshot
93	```
94	
95	`WORKSPACE_ADMIN_EMAILS` defaults to `dev-bypass@dataq.local,${DATAQ_SIGNIN_EMAIL}`
96	— so every signed-in address is workspace-admin by default, which is what
97	gives a freshly-provisioned local user visibility into prod's suites (they
98	belong to prod's *user rows*, not to whichever new email you sign in with;
99	workspace-admin has implicit visibility into everything, ADR 0027).
100	
101	### 2.3 Mirror OpenBao onto Key Vault (exact set, no extras)
102	
103	```bash
104	KV=dataq-app-kv-aw6laj   # re-verify with `az keyvault list` in case it's been renamed
105	source .env.app          # OPENBAO_ADDR / OPENBAO_MOUNT / OPENBAO_TOKEN
106	
107	az keyvault secret list --vault-name "$KV" --query "[?attributes.enabled].name" -o tsv | sort > /tmp/kv_names.txt
108	
109	curl -s -H "X-Vault-Token: $OPENBAO_TOKEN" "$OPENBAO_ADDR/v1/$OPENBAO_MOUNT/metadata?list=true" \
110	  | python3 -c "import json,sys; print('\n'.join(sorted(json.load(sys.stdin)['data']['keys'])))" > /tmp/local_names.txt
111	
112	# purge anything local-only
113	comm -23 /tmp/local_names.txt /tmp/kv_names.txt | while read -r n; do
114	  curl -s -o /dev/null -X DELETE -H "X-Vault-Token: $OPENBAO_TOKEN" "$OPENBAO_ADDR/v1/$OPENBAO_MOUNT/metadata/$n"
115	done
116	
117	# write in every KV secret (value piped straight through, never echoed/printed)
118	while read -r n; do
119	  az keyvault secret show --vault-name "$KV" --name "$n" --query value -o tsv \
120	    | python3 -c "import sys,json; print(json.dumps({'data':{'value': sys.stdin.readline().rstrip(chr(10))}}))" \
121	    | curl -s -o /dev/null -X POST -H "X-Vault-Token: $OPENBAO_TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
122	      --data-binary @- "$OPENBAO_ADDR/v1/$OPENBAO_MOUNT/data/$n"
123	done < /tmp/kv_names.txt
124	```
125	
126	**Gotcha:** this purge also deletes `dataq-local-smtp` — the bundled Mailpit
127	catcher's password, seeded locally by the one-shot `otp-mail-secret` compose
128	service. It never exists in prod Key Vault by design (prod mails via Gmail
129	SMTP under different secret names), so a strict "match KV exactly" diff
130	always removes it, and OTP sign-in then fails with
131	`otp_email_not_configured`. Fix, every time:
132	
133	```bash
134	docker compose up -d --force-recreate otp-mail-secret
135	```
136	
137	### 2.4 Wipe local seed data, pull in prod's real data
138	
139	```bash
140	cd ~/Coding/Python/DataQ
141	
142	# 1. temp access to the shared prod Postgres server
143	MYIP=$(curl -s https://api.ipify.org)
144	az postgres flexible-server firewall-rule create -g dataq-rg --server-name dataq-pg-wus3-3erlgd \
145	  --name "temp-local-sync-$(python3 -c 'import time;print(int(time.time()))')" \
146	  --start-ip-address "$MYIP" --end-ip-address "$MYIP"
147	
148	# 2. resolve prod's DATABASE_URL — it is NOT in any tfvars file (apply-time-only var);
149	#    read it straight off the live Container App secret instead:
150	export PROD_DATABASE_URL=$(az containerapp secret list -n dataq-app-api -g dataq-rg --show-values -o json \
151	  | python3 -c "import json,sys; d=json.load(sys.stdin); print(next(s['value'] for s in d if s['name']=='database-url'))")
152	
153	# 3. nuke local schema, re-migrate (NO reseed — that's exactly the demo data being removed)
154	docker compose exec -T postgres psql -U dataq -d dataq -c "DROP SCHEMA public CASCADE; CREATE SCHEMA public;"
155	export LOCAL_DATABASE_URL="REDACTED"
156	(cd backend && DATABASE_URL="$LOCAL_DATABASE_URL" conda run -n dataq alembic upgrade head)
157	# Gotcha: `conda run -n dataq sh -c "cd backend && alembic upgrade head"` alone fails with
158	# "no password supplied" — pydantic-settings' env_file=".env.app" resolves relative to cwd,
159	# and there is no backend/.env.app (only the repo-root one). Export DATABASE_URL explicitly.
160	
161	# 4. copy users -> connections -> suites -> checks, in that FK order
162	conda run -n dataq python /path/to/sync_prod_data.py   # script below
163	
164	# 5. close the firewall rule immediately
165	RULE=$(az postgres flexible-server firewall-rule list -g dataq-rg --server-name dataq-pg-wus3-3erlgd \
166	  --query "[?starts_with(name,'temp-local-sync-')].name" -o tsv)
167	az postgres flexible-server firewall-rule delete -g dataq-rg --server-name dataq-pg-wus3-3erlgd --name "$RULE" --yes
168	```
169	
170	`sync_prod_data.py` (generic reflection-based copy, JSONB-safe, nulls
171	`asset_id` since `assets` is out of scope):
172	
173	```python
174	import os, sys
175	import psycopg2
176	import psycopg2.extras
177	
178	PROD_URL = os.environ["PROD_DATABASE_URL"].replace("postgresql+psycopg2://", "postgresql://")
179	LOCAL_URL = os.environ["LOCAL_DATABASE_URL"].replace("postgresql+psycopg2://", "postgresql://")
180	TABLES = ["users", "connections", "suites", "checks"]   # FK order
181	
182	prod = psycopg2.connect(PROD_URL); prod.set_session(readonly=True, autocommit=True)
183	local = psycopg2.connect(LOCAL_URL); local.autocommit = False
184	
185	try:
186	    with local.cursor() as lcur:
187	        for table in TABLES:
188	            with prod.cursor(cursor_factory=psycopg2.extras.RealDictCursor) as pcur:
189	                pcur.execute(f"SELECT * FROM {table}")
190	                rows = pcur.fetchall()
191	            if not rows:
192	                print(f"{table}: 0 rows, skipping"); continue
193	            cols = list(rows[0].keys())
194	            if "asset_id" in cols:
195	                for r in rows: r["asset_id"] = None
196	            for r in rows:
197	                for k, v in r.items():
198	                    if isinstance(v, (dict, list)):
199	                        r[k] = psycopg2.extras.Json(v)
200	            col_list = ", ".join(f'"{c}"' for c in cols)
201	            placeholders = ", ".join(f"%({c})s" for c in cols)
202	            psycopg2.extras.execute_batch(
203	                lcur, f'INSERT INTO {table} ({col_list}) VALUES ({placeholders})', rows
204	            )
205	            print(f"{table}: inserted {len(rows)} rows")
206	    local.commit(); print("COMMIT ok")
207	except Exception:
208	    local.rollback(); raise
209	finally:
210	    prod.close(); local.close()
211	```
212	
213	### 2.5 Backfill assets + fix the lineage watermark (after the copy, every time)
214	
215	The copy above bypasses `suite_service`, so `assets` stays empty until you
216	force a resolve. For every suite, `PATCH` it with its **own current**
217	`target` (fetch via `GET /suites`, resend the same `target` dict — `None`
218	means "unchanged" in this API, so you must resend it explicitly to trigger
219	resolution):
220	
221	```bash
222	curl -s -b cookies.txt -X PATCH "http://localhost:8000/api/v1/suites/$SUITE_ID" \
223	  -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d "{\"target\": $TARGET_JSON}"
224	```
225	
226	Then reset the UC lineage watermark so a future warehouse-lineage refresh
227	doesn't silently skip history it never actually has locally:
228	
229	```bash
230	docker compose exec -T postgres psql -U dataq -d dataq -c \
231	  "UPDATE connections SET lineage_watermark = NULL, lineage_last_refresh_at = NULL, lineage_last_tier = NULL WHERE type = 'unity_catalog';"
232	```
233	
234	(Snowflake connections don't need this — their lineage pull is a full
235	snapshot re-read each time, not incremental.)
236	
237	---
238	
239	## 3. Using this mirror for local testing
240	
241	Once §2 is done, the local stack behaves like a real, working copy of prod:
242	
243	- **Sign in** at `http://localhost:3000` (or via the OTP API directly:
244	  `POST /api/v1/auth/otp/request` → read the code at
245	  `http://localhost:8025` → `POST /api/v1/auth/otp/verify`).
246	- **All 13 real connections and 12 real suites** are there, pointed at the
247	  actual live Snowflake/ADLS/UC/ADF/Airflow/dbt/Iceberg endpoints — a suite
248	  run genuinely queries the live warehouse, same as it would in prod. Trigger
249	  one with `POST /suites/{id}/run`, poll `GET /runs/{id}`.
250	- **Connection tests** (`POST /connections/{id}/test`) are a fast, read-only
251	  way to confirm the OpenBao mirror is intact without running a full suite.
252	- **Assets/lineage**: the asset view (`GET /assets/{id}`) works normally —
253	  scorecard, dimension coverage, linked suites. Lineage edges stay empty
254	  unless you flip `WAREHOUSE_LINEAGE_ENABLED=true` in `.env.app` and either
255	  wait for the daily `02:37 UTC` beat task or trigger
256	  `refresh_warehouse_lineage` manually via a Celery call.
257	- **What won't work**: cron schedules and orchestration triggers, since
258	  `schedules`/`trigger_bindings` weren't copied (§1). A suite will only run
259	  when you trigger it manually.
260	- **Re-syncing later**: OpenBao is **dev-mode / in-memory** — it loses
261	  everything on `docker compose down` or a container restart. Re-run §2.3
262	  after any restart. The DB copy in §2.4 is durable (real Postgres volume)
263	  until you next reset it.
264	
265	---
266	
267	## 4. Utilizing the local Airflow + MinIO stack
268	
269	**As of this session, they are up but genuinely unused** — none of the 13
270	prod-mirrored connections point at them (they all point at the real Azure
271	endpoints, matching prod). MinIO's `landing` bucket and the Airflow scheduler
272	still hold state from an **older** session (mockdata seeded 2026-07-27; DAG
273	runs `flow_a_snowflake_load` / `flow_a_uc_reference` / `flow_b_medallion`
274	last shown `failed` from that same old run) — nothing from the 2026-08-03
275	session touched them.
276	
277	To actually exercise them, two independent things need to happen:
278	
279	**A. Re-seed / re-run the harness itself** (tests the ETL flow in isolation,
280	nothing to do with DataQ yet):
281	
282	```bash
283	cd ~/Coding/Python/DataQ-harness/local
284	./harness_local.sh seed          # backfill mockdata -> MinIO
285	./harness_local.sh run --dags    # unpause + REST-trigger the cron DAGs
286	./harness_local.sh status        # container + DAG state
287	```
288	
289	Airflow UI: `http://localhost:8080` (admin / see `local/.env`). MinIO
290	console: `http://localhost:9001`.
291	
292	**B. Point a DataQ connection at them** (this is what actually puts them in
293	DataQ's monitoring path — see the harness README's "Point DataQ at it"
294	section for the full detail, summarized here):
295	
296	- **MinIO as an `s3` connection** (DataQ #1063, ordinary `s3` connection
297	  type, no special local mode): `bucket=landing`, `region=us-east-1`,
298	  `endpoint_url=http://minio:9000`, access key/secret =
299	  `MINIO_ROOT_USER`/`MINIO_ROOT_PASSWORD` (from `local/.env`). Leave
300	  addressing style `auto` — it resolves to **path** style automatically
301	  because an endpoint is set (MinIO only serves the bucket in the path).
302	- **Local Airflow as an `airflow` connection**: `base_url=http://airflow-webserver:8080`,
303	  basic auth, user `admin`, password from `local/.env`.
304	
305	Either create these as **new, additional** local-only connections/suites (so
306	you don't disturb the prod-mirrored ones), or temporarily repoint one of the
307	mirrored flat-file/orchestration connections at the local endpoints if you
308	specifically want to compare local vs. prod behavior on the same suite
309	definition.
310	
311	This combination (§4A + §4B) was **validated end-to-end once already**, on
312	2026-07-27, before this session (see DataQ's `docs/ops-log.md`): 4 DAGs
313	parsed clean, 24 datasets seeded, DataQ connection test green, flat-file
314	suite 4/4 (643 rows, arrival-time freshness read off MinIO's
315	`LastModified`), `flow_a_snowflake_load` succeeded into live Snowflake, and
316	DataQ ingested the local DAG runs into `pipeline_runs`. That state is what's
317	currently sitting stale in the containers — re-running §4A brings it current
318	again; §4B (the DataQ-side connection) was not re-created this session and
319	would need to be added again if you want DataQ itself watching the local
320	harness rather than just the harness running standalone.
321	
322	---
323	
324	## 5. Teardown
325	
326	```bash
327	# local harness
328	cd ~/Coding/Python/DataQ-harness/local
329	./harness_local.sh down            # add --volumes to also drop the metadata DB + MinIO data
330	
331	# DataQ stack
332	cd ~/Coding/Python/DataQ
333	docker compose down                 # add -v to also drop Postgres/OpenBao data
334	```
335	
336	Nothing here touches Azure/prod — every prod-facing action in §2 is either
337	read-only (`az keyvault secret show`, the prod `SELECT`s) or explicitly
338	scoped and reverted (the firewall rule).
339

belong to prod's *user rows*, not to whichever new email you sign in with;
workspace-admin has implicit visibility into everything, ADR 0027).

### 2.3 Mirror OpenBao onto Key Vault (exact set, no extras)

```bash
KV=dataq-app-kv-aw6laj   # re-verify with `az keyvault list` in case it's been renamed
source .env.app          # OPENBAO_ADDR / OPENBAO_MOUNT / OPENBAO_TOKEN

az keyvault secret list --vault-name "$KV" --query "[?attributes.enabled].name" -o tsv | sort > /tmp/kv_names.txt

curl -s -H "X-Vault-Token: $OPENBAO_TOKEN" "$OPENBAO_ADDR/v1/$OPENBAO_MOUNT/metadata?list=true" \
  | python3 -c "import json,sys; print('\n'.join(sorted(json.load(sys.stdin)['data']['keys'])))" > /tmp/local_names.txt

# purge anything local-only
comm -23 /tmp/local_names.txt /tmp/kv_names.txt | while read -r n; do
  curl -s -o /dev/null -X DELETE -H "X-Vault-Token: $OPENBAO_TOKEN" "$OPENBAO_ADDR/v1/$OPENBAO_MOUNT/metadata/$n"
done

# write in every KV secret (value piped straight through, never echoed/printed)
while read -r n; do
  az keyvault secret show --vault-name "$KV" --name "$n" --query value -o tsv \
    | python3 -c "import sys,json; print(json.dumps({'data':{'value': sys.stdin.readline().rstrip(chr(10))}}))" \
    | curl -s -o /dev/null -X POST -H "X-Vault-Token: $OPENBAO_TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
      --data-binary @- "$OPENBAO_ADDR/v1/$OPENBAO_MOUNT/data/$n"
done < /tmp/kv_names.txt
```

**Gotcha:** this purge also deletes `dataq-local-smtp` — the bundled Mailpit
catcher's password, seeded locally by the one-shot `otp-mail-secret` compose
service. It never exists in prod Key Vault by design (prod mails via Gmail
SMTP under different secret names), so a strict "match KV exactly" diff
always removes it, and OTP sign-in then fails with
`otp_email_not_configured`. Fix, every time:

```bash
docker compose up -d --force-recreate otp-mail-secret
```

### 2.4 Wipe local seed data, pull in prod's real data

```bash
cd ~/Coding/Python/DataQ

# 1. temp access to the shared prod Postgres server
MYIP=$(curl -s https://api.ipify.org)
az postgres flexible-server firewall-rule create -g dataq-rg --server-name dataq-pg-wus3-3erlgd \
  --name "temp-local-sync-$(python3 -c 'import time;print(int(time.time()))')" \
  --start-ip-address "$MYIP" --end-ip-address "$MYIP"

# 2. resolve prod's DATABASE_URL — it is NOT in any tfvars file (apply-time-only var);
#    read it straight off the live Container App secret instead:
export PROD_DATABASE_URL=$(az containerapp secret list -n dataq-app-api -g dataq-rg --show-values -o json \
  | python3 -c "import json,sys; d=json.load(sys.stdin); print(next(s['value'] for s in d if s['name']=='database-url'))")

# 3. nuke local schema, re-migrate (NO reseed — that's exactly the demo data being removed)
docker compose exec -T postgres psql -U dataq -d dataq -c "DROP SCHEMA public CASCADE; CREATE SCHEMA public;"
export LOCAL_DATABASE_URL="REDACTED"
(cd backend && DATABASE_URL="$LOCAL_DATABASE_URL" conda run -n dataq alembic upgrade head)
# Gotcha: `conda run -n dataq sh -c "cd backend && alembic upgrade head"` alone fails with
# "no password supplied" — pydantic-settings' env_file=".env.app" resolves relative to cwd,
# and there is no backend/.env.app (only the repo-root one). Export DATABASE_URL explicitly.

# 4. copy users -> connections -> suites -> checks, in that FK order
conda run -n dataq python /path/to/sync_prod_data.py   # script below

# 5. close the firewall rule immediately
RULE=$(az postgres flexible-server firewall-rule list -g dataq-rg --server-name dataq-pg-wus3-3erlgd \
  --query "[?starts_with(name,'temp-local-sync-')].name" -o tsv)
az postgres flexible-server firewall-rule delete -g dataq-rg --server-name dataq-pg-wus3-3erlgd --name "$RULE" --yes
```

`sync_prod_data.py` (generic reflection-based copy, JSONB-safe, nulls
`asset_id` since `assets` is out of scope):

```python
import os, sys
import psycopg2
import psycopg2.extras

PROD_URL = os.environ["PROD_DATABASE_URL"].replace("postgresql+psycopg2://", "postgresql://")
LOCAL_URL = os.environ["LOCAL_DATABASE_URL"].replace("postgresql+psycopg2://", "postgresql://")
TABLES = ["users", "connections", "suites", "checks"]   # FK order

prod = psycopg2.connect(PROD_URL); prod.set_session(readonly=True, autocommit=True)
local = psycopg2.connect(LOCAL_URL); local.autocommit = False

try:
    with local.cursor() as lcur:
        for table in TABLES:
            with prod.cursor(cursor_factory=psycopg2.extras.RealDictCursor) as pcur:
                pcur.execute(f"SELECT * FROM {table}")
                rows = pcur.fetchall()
            if not rows:
                print(f"{table}: 0 rows, skipping"); continue
            cols = list(rows[0].keys())
            if "asset_id" in cols:
                for r in rows: r["asset_id"] = None
            for r in rows:
                for k, v in r.items():
                    if isinstance(v, (dict, list)):
                        r[k] = psycopg2.extras.Json(v)
            col_list = ", ".join(f'"{c}"' for c in cols)
            placeholders = ", ".join(f"%({c})s" for c in cols)
            psycopg2.extras.execute_batch(
                lcur, f'INSERT INTO {table} ({col_list}) VALUES ({placeholders})', rows
            )
            print(f"{table}: inserted {len(rows)} rows")
    local.commit(); print("COMMIT ok")
except Exception:
    local.rollback(); raise
finally:
    prod.close(); local.close()
```

### 2.5 Backfill assets + fix the lineage watermark (after the copy, every time)

The copy above bypasses `suite_service`, so `assets` stays empty until you
force a resolve. For every suite, `PATCH` it with its **own current**
`target` (fetch via `GET /suites`, resend the same `target` dict — `None`
means "unchanged" in this API, so you must resend it explicitly to trigger
resolution):

```bash
curl -s -b cookies.txt -X PATCH "http://localhost:8000/api/v1/suites/$SUITE_ID" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d "{\"target\": $TARGET_JSON}"
```

Then reset the UC lineage watermark so a future warehouse-lineage refresh
doesn't silently skip history it never actually has locally:

```bash
docker compose exec -T postgres psql -U dataq -d dataq -c \
  "UPDATE connections SET lineage_watermark = NULL, lineage_last_refresh_at = NULL, lineage_last_tier = NULL WHERE type = 'unity_catalog';"
```

(Snowflake connections don't need this — their lineage pull is a full
snapshot re-read each time, not incremental.)

---

## 3. Using this mirror for local testing

Once §2 is done, the local stack behaves like a real, working copy of prod:

- **Sign in** at `http://localhost:3000` (or via the OTP API directly:
  `POST /api/v1/auth/otp/request` → read the code at
  `http://localhost:8025` → `POST /api/v1/auth/otp/verify`).
- **All 13 real connections and 12 real suites** are there, pointed at the
  actual live Snowflake/ADLS/UC/ADF/Airflow/dbt/Iceberg endpoints — a suite
  run genuinely queries the live warehouse, same as it would in prod. Trigger
  one with `POST /suites/{id}/run`, poll `GET /runs/{id}`.
- **Connection tests** (`POST /connections/{id}/test`) are a fast, read-only
  way to confirm the OpenBao mirror is intact without running a full suite.
- **Assets/lineage**: the asset view (`GET /assets/{id}`) works normally —
  scorecard, dimension coverage, linked suites. Lineage edges stay empty
  unless you flip `WAREHOUSE_LINEAGE_ENABLED=true` in `.env.app` and either
  wait for the daily `02:37 UTC` beat task or trigger
  `refresh_warehouse_lineage` manually via a Celery call.
- **What won't work**: cron schedules and orchestration triggers, since
  `schedules`/`trigger_bindings` weren't copied (§1). A suite will only run
  when you trigger it manually.
- **Re-syncing later**: OpenBao is **dev-mode / in-memory** — it loses
  everything on `docker compose down` or a container restart. Re-run §2.3
  after any restart. The DB copy in §2.4 is durable (real Postgres volume)
  until you next reset it.

---

## 4. Utilizing the local Airflow + MinIO stack

**As of this session, they are up but genuinely unused** — none of the 13
prod-mirrored connections point at them (they all point at the real Azure
endpoints, matching prod). MinIO's `landing` bucket and the Airflow scheduler
still hold state from an **older** session (mockdata seeded 2026-07-27; DAG
runs `flow_a_snowflake_load` / `flow_a_uc_reference` / `flow_b_medallion`
last shown `failed` from that same old run) — nothing from the 2026-08-03
session touched them.

To actually exercise them, two independent things need to happen:

**A. Re-seed / re-run the harness itself** (tests the ETL flow in isolation,
nothing to do with DataQ yet):

```bash
cd ~/Coding/Python/DataQ-harness/local
./harness_local.sh seed          # backfill mockdata -> MinIO
./harness_local.sh run --dags    # unpause + REST-trigger the cron DAGs
./harness_local.sh status        # container + DAG state
```

Airflow UI: `http://localhost:8080` (admin / see `local/.env`). MinIO
console: `http://localhost:9001`.

**B. Point a DataQ connection at them** (this is what actually puts them in
DataQ's monitoring path — see the harness README's "Point DataQ at it"
section for the full detail, summarized here):

- **MinIO as an `s3` connection** (DataQ #1063, ordinary `s3` connection
  type, no special local mode): `bucket=landing`, `region=us-east-1`,
  `endpoint_url=http://minio:9000`, access key/secret =
  `MINIO_ROOT_USER`/`MINIO_ROOT_PASSWORD` (from `local/.env`). Leave
  addressing style `auto` — it resolves to **path** style automatically
  because an endpoint is set (MinIO only serves the bucket in the path).
- **Local Airflow as an `airflow` connection**: `base_url=http://airflow-webserver:8080`,
  basic auth, user `admin`, password from `local/.env`.

Either create these as **new, additional** local-only connections/suites (so
you don't disturb the prod-mirrored ones), or temporarily repoint one of the
mirrored flat-file/orchestration connections at the local endpoints if you
specifically want to compare local vs. prod behavior on the same suite
definition.

This combination (§4A + §4B) was **validated end-to-end once already**, on
2026-07-27, before this session (see DataQ's `docs/ops-log.md`): 4 DAGs
parsed clean, 24 datasets seeded, DataQ connection test green, flat-file
suite 4/4 (643 rows, arrival-time freshness read off MinIO's
`LastModified`), `flow_a_snowflake_load` succeeded into live Snowflake, and
DataQ ingested the local DAG runs into `pipeline_runs`. That state is what's
currently sitting stale in the containers — re-running §4A brings it current
again; §4B (the DataQ-side connection) was not re-created this session and
would need to be added again if you want DataQ itself watching the local
harness rather than just the harness running standalone.

---

## 5. Teardown

```bash
# local harness
cd ~/Coding/Python/DataQ-harness/local
./harness_local.sh down            # add --volumes to also drop the metadata DB + MinIO data

# DataQ stack
cd ~/Coding/Python/DataQ
docker compose down                 # add -v to also drop Postgres/OpenBao data
```

Nothing here touches Azure/prod — every prod-facing action in §2 is either
read-only (`az keyvault secret show`, the prod `SELECT`s) or explicitly
scoped and reverted (the firewall rule).

# harness_local.sh — drive the LOCAL, Azure-free harness stack.
#
# The counterpart to ../scripts/harness_window.sh, which opens a test window on
# Azure. Same flows, no subscription: Airflow (Postgres + Redis + CeleryExecutor)
# and a MinIO landing zone, running the same image and the same DAGs.
#
# Usage:
#   harness_local.sh up                 # generate .env if missing, build, start, wait healthy
#   harness_local.sh seed [--tier S]    # backfill the mockdata feeds into MinIO
#   harness_local.sh run [--dags]       # --dags: unpause + REST-trigger the cron DAGs
#   harness_local.sh status             # container + DAG state (read-only)
#   harness_local.sh snowflake          # start the Snowflake stand-in (fakesnow)
#                                       #   and probe it with DataQ's real code
#                                       #   paths. CONTINUITY, not coverage —
#                                       #   see snowflake_probe.py.
#   harness_local.sh down [--volumes]   # stop; --volumes also drops the data
#
# Requires DataQ's own stack to be up (this joins its `dataq_default` network).
#
---

content.content:
"""Flow D — Apache Iceberg writer (no orchestrator).

Each ``iceberg-tick`` appends a referentially-consistent batch of purchase-order
rows to the Iceberg table ``retail.purchase_orders`` via a pyiceberg **SqlCatalog**
(Postgres-backed metadata) with an **ADLS (abfss) warehouse** read through
fsspec/adlfs. DataQ reads the same table **natively** (its ``iceberg`` connection,
ADR 0030) on its own DataQ schedule — there is **no orchestrator and no
trigger-binding** (the Flow-C precedent: nothing "loads" this for DataQ to react to).

Self-contained by design — unlike the ``tick`` feeds this needs **no persisted
state file**. Each tick simply appends another snapshot (idempotent-safe: re-running
just adds another batch). ``po_id`` is namespaced by the tick's wall-clock so two
ticks never collide (which would forge an *accidental* duplicate and muddy the one
*deliberate* duplicate we seed). Supplier / product ids come from the same seeded
pools idiom (``rng.id_pool``) the rest of the harness uses, so they read as the same
id space as Flow A's ``suppliers`` / ``products``.

Seeded DQ issues per tick (mirrors ``dq_issues.py`` rates/style) give DataQ's checks
something real to bite on: ~1-2% negative ``order_qty`` (fails a ``order_qty >= 0``
range check), ~1% null ``supplier_id`` (fails ``not_null supplier_id``), and a rare
duplicate ``(po_id, po_line)`` (fails a uniqueness check).

The pyiceberg / pyarrow imports are module-local to the functions that need a live
catalog so ``python -m mockdata --help`` (and the other subcommands) don't pay for
them; ``iceberg-tick`` is the only path that requires the Iceberg deps.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import datetime as dt
import os
from typing import Any

from .rng import Rng

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Table coordinates + generation shape.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

NAMESPACE = "retail"
TABLE = "purchase_orders"
IDENTIFIER = f"{NAMESPACE}.{TABLE}"

# Referential pools (same id shapes as Flow A: SUP-#### width 4, SKU-###### width 6).
N_SUPPLIERS = 30
N_PRODUCTS = 200

# Batch sizing + issue rates (mirror dq_issues.py: low single-digit %).
DEFAULT_ROWS_MIN = 200
DEFAULT_ROWS_MAX = 500
NEG_QTY_RATE = 0.015  # ~1.5% negative order_qty
NULL_SUPPLIER_RATE = 0.01  # ~1% null supplier_id
DUP_RATE = 0.005  # ~0.5% duplicated (po_id, po_line) rows

PO_STATUSES = ["open", "partial", "received", "cancelled"]
CURRENCIES = ["USD", "EUR", "GBP", "CAD", "JPY"]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Catalog wiring.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def catalog_properties_from_env() -> dict[str, str]:
    """Compose ``load_catalog`` / ``SqlCatalog`` properties from the Job's env.

    ``ICEBERG_CATALOG_URI`` (the Postgres SQLAlchemy DSN, secret) + ``ICEBERG_WAREHOUSE``
    (the ``abfss://iceberg@<acct>.dfs.core.windows.net/warehouse`` root) + the ADLS
    account name/key for the fsspec (adlfs) FileIO. Mirrors the DataQ ``iceberg``
    connection's own catalog properties (``IcebergConfig.catalog_properties``) so both
    sides read the same table the same way.
    """
    uri = os.environ["ICEBERG_CATALOG_URI"]
    warehouse = os.environ["ICEBERG_WAREHOUSE"]
    props: dict[str, str] = {
        "uri": uri,
        "warehouse": warehouse,
        # Native (no query engine) object-store IO through fsspec/adlfs.
        "py-io-impl": "pyiceberg.io.fsspec.FsspecFileIO",
    }

        DoubleType,

        NestedField,
        StringType,
        TimestamptzType,

    return Schema(

input.description: Real-user Playwright QA across datasources
input.prompt:
DataQ's local dev stack is up at http://localhost:3000 (frontend) / http://localhost:8000 (api), running the LATEST code (commit 1758cf8a, 56 commits ahead of what's in prod). We're about to deploy this delta to production and need thorough real-user QA first — no shortcuts via direct DB edits, everything through the real UI (Playwright) as an actual signed-in user would do it. This is a long, multi-part task — take your time, work through it systematically, and don't skip steps due to friction; work around blockers.

## Sign-in
Local stack uses email-OTP auth. Two allowed users are configured: `admin@dataq.com` (the sole workspace admin) and `user.01@dataq.com` (an ordinary non-admin user). To sign in: on the frontend's sign-in page, enter the email, request a code, then fetch the code from Mailpit (the local mail catcher) at http://localhost:8025 — either its web UI or `curl -s http://localhost:8025/api/v1/messages | python3 -m json.tool` to find the latest message to that address and extract the 6-digit code from its body, then enter it in the UI's verify step.

## Part 1 — as admin@dataq.com: create 4 real connections via the UI's "Add Connection" drawer
For each, you'll need real credential material. NEVER print, log, or include secret values in your final report or any file you write — fetch them inline and paste directly into the Playwright form-fill call, nothing more.

1. **Snowflake** — account `PVQSOEQ-ZGB34383`, user `ROYARIJIT04`, role `DATAQ_READER`, database `DATAQ_DB`, schema `RETAIL`, warehouse `DATAQ_WH`. The credential (private key, likely PEM) is in local OpenBao (dev-mode HTTP API) — read `~/Coding/Python/DataQ/.env.app` for `OPENBAO_ADDR`/`OPENBAO_MOUNT`/`OPENBAO_TOKEN`, then `curl -s -H "X-Vault-Token: $OPENBAO_TOKEN" "$OPENBAO_ADDR/v1/$OPENBAO_MOUNT/data/conn-snowflake-analytics-dev-7a29affe"` (or try the QA-suffixed sibling `conn-snowflake-analytics-qa-2da4a2e8` if the first doesn't parse as a key) to get the real credential JSON. Whatever the connection form's auth-mode field expects (password vs key-pair), match it to what the fetched secret looks like.
2. **Unity Catalog (Databricks)** — workspace `https://dbc-4492dde4-090c.cloud.databricks.com`, warehouse http_path `/sql/1.0/warehouses/b6403b6e3734f0ce`, catalog `dataq_retail`. PAT token is in OpenBao under `conn-unity-catalog-uc-lakehouse-uat-0c82857b` (fetch same way as above).
3. **S3 (MinIO flatfile)** — ordinary `s3` connection type, `bucket=landing`, `region=us-east-1`, `endpoint_url=http://minio:9000` (reachable by container name — DataQ's api/worker joined the harness's docker network), access key = `MINIO_ROOT_USER` and secret = `MINIO_ROOT_PASSWORD` from `~/Coding/Python/DataQ-harness/local/.env` (read that file directly, it's local dev-only). Leave addressing style `auto`.
4. **Iceberg** — this is a native `pyiceberg` connection (ADR 0030), NOT an s3 connection type — look for "Iceberg" in the Add Connection type list. Config: `catalog_type=sql`, `catalog_uri=postgresql+psycopg2://dataq@postgres:5432/iceberg_catalog` (NO password embedded in the URI — the form has a separate password/secret field, put `dataq` there), `warehouse=s3://iceberg/warehouse`, `catalog_name=harness` (must be exactly `harness`, not `default`). It'll also need S3-endpoint fields for MinIO — look for endpoint/access-key/secret-key fields on the form (same MinIO creds as #3, endpoint `http://minio:9000`, path-style addressing). The table that should resolve is `retail.purchase_orders` (already seeded with ~1758 rows). If the form doesn't obviously expose S3-endpoint override fields, read `backend/app/datasources/iceberg.py`'s `IcebergConfig` class and the connections type-catalog (frontend `frontend/src/`) to find the actual field names before giving up.

Test each connection (the form's own "Test connection" button) before saving. Note any friction, unclear labels, or errors as findings — that's real signal for a real-user QA pass.

## Part 2 — as admin@dataq.com: author suites + checks via UI (Monaco/check editor, not API)
For each of the 4 connections, create one suite with 2-4 checks covering a mix of check kinds if the UI supports it easily (not_null / range / freshness are enough — don't force anomaly/comparison/schema_drift unless straightforward). Use real tables: Snowflake `RETAIL.ORDERS_HEADER`, UC `dataq_retail.gold.feedback_sentiment` (check what schemas/tables actually exist if this guess is wrong — browse via the UI's target picker), S3 flatfile — the MinIO `landing` bucket has ~24 seeded CSV datasets (e.g. `orders_header`, `products`, `tracking_events` — browse via the UI), Iceberg `retail.purchase_orders`. Then **trigger a run** for each suite from the UI ("Run now") and watch it complete via the live-progress drawer, then open the run detail page.

## Part 3 — verify the column-stretch fix delta specifically
Issue #1184 (pipeline-runs "Failure reason" column) was already fixed and IS in prod. What's NOT yet in prod is PR #1208 — the RunDetail page's "Observed" column (`observed_value`) getting the same bounded-width+tooltip treatment for `schema_drift`/`comparison` check kinds, whose observed_value can be a long list/dict. If you have time, author one `schema_drift` or `comparison` check (target a table with several columns) so its observed_value is a longer structure, run it, and open the run-detail page — confirm the Observed column stays a fixed width with an ellipsis + hover tooltip instead of stretching the table. Screenshot if you can. If authoring those check kinds proves too time-consuming, it's fine to just visually confirm the column definition behaves correctly on whatever check results you do have, and note that the long-observed_value case wasn't specifically exercised.

## Part 4 — as user.01@dataq.com: non-admin real-user pass
Sign out, sign in as `user.01@dataq.com`. Confirm: no `/admin` nav item and a 403/Forbidden if you navigate there directly; the workspace is empty (no visibility into admin's suites/connections, since nothing's shared yet) OR whatever the actual real behavior is — report what you see, don't assume. Then, as this user, create one connection + suite of your own (pick the easiest datasource, e.g. the S3 MinIO one) end-to-end via the UI, run it, view results — this is the "brand new ordinary user" experience end to end.

## Part 5 — general UI health pass
While you're in there, exercise: Results page + pipeline-runs tab, Dashboard, Connections list, Suites list/detail, run-detail page, check version-history drawer, and note ANY rendering bugs, console errors, broken layouts, or confusing UX — not just the specific fixes above. Check both desktop viewport and a mobile viewport per your normal practice.

## Report
Structure your final report as: (1) connection setup results per datasource (pass/fail/friction), (2) suite authoring + run results per datasource, (3) the #1208 Observed-column verification specifically, (4) admin vs non-admin behavior findings, (5) any other bugs/UX issues found, each tagged with severity. This feeds a go/no-go decision for a production deploy, so be concrete about what would block a deploy vs what's a minor follow-up.

### 2. Test-quality audit (Mode 2) — fix commits, 7018d772..HEAD

The 56 commits skew heavily toward `fix:` (~23) with a handful of `feat:`/`chore:`/`docs:`. This is an unusually disciplined batch: every fix commit I sampled includes `Fixes #N`, a real-object test (not a mock of the seam under test), and several explicitly record mutation-checking of the new assertions in the commit body. Spot-checked the highest-risk (data-ingestion / redaction-adjacent) fixes in depth:

- `b23b3f7b` (bound+redact list-shaped GX `observed_value`, #1229) — caps at capture in `gx_runner.py`, re-derives/redacts at read time in `run_service.py` for pre-fix rows already in prod. Tests in `test_gx_runner.py`/`test_run_service.py` (+133/+58 lines) exercise both capture and read paths, including the correction of already-persisted oversized rows.
- `112821a2` (PII classifier evidence-window regression fix, #1230) — this is the standout: fixes a *previous* fix (#1196's sample cap) that had silently narrowed the PII detection window and could misclassify a genuinely-PII column as safe to show. New `_valid_summary` cross-field consistency check plus an explicit `OverflowError` fix found live (`"n": 1e400` → `int()` crash → 500) — the commit message states both new assertions were mutation-checked by reverting the fix and confirming the test failed for the right reason, then restoring. This is exactly the discipline CONTRIBUTING rule 4a asks for.
- `5c676952` (retention sweep for list-shaped `observed_value`, #1253) — extends purge coverage with a `jsonb_typeof` guard so scalar aggregates (which back `metric_value` trends per ADR 0012) are never touched; test asserts the retention_days≤0 guard covers both sibling columns. Deliberately scoped a known adjacent gap out and filed it (#1267) rather than scope-creeping.
- `d293399d` (strip SQL/parameter-echo from persisted GX error, #1203) — builds tests against a **real** `sqlalchemy.exc.StatementError`, not a hand-written string, and asserts the premise (parameter present in raw message) before asserting it's stripped — avoids the "tests a string I imagined" trap.
- `4605aa4c` (phantom health_alerted_at stamp, #1101/#1225) — fixes a real alerting-suppression bug (an incident could be permanently silenced with zero notifications ever sent) using the "delivered-first" contract already established by a prior fix (#1100), with a shared `_fan_out_delivered_first` extraction to prevent the two call sites drifting again. Deferred the double-logged-traceback finding to #1226, which itself later shipped as `aa22c651` in this same batch.
- `580efe6f` / `ef47b80c` (connect_timeout / TCP keepalives on the shared DB engine) — mirrors the fix onto the separate migrate-job engine (alembic `env.py`) after review caught the parity gap; the keepalives commit is honest that it's **not** verified against a real black-holed connection and records that as an explicitly open gap rather than claiming full coverage.
- `cc70766b` (zero-table inventory sync vs never-synced, #1242) — new nullable columns give "0 tables" an honest state distinct from "never synced," with 8 test methods (`TestZeroTableEnumeration`) covering the N>0→0 transition specifically (the privilege-loss/dropped-DB signal is the actual risk).

**No hard findings (🔴) in this diff.** No mocked-seam-under-test smells found in the sampled commits — tests mock below the seam (SQLAlchemy exceptions, secret store, HTTP publishers) not the module under test itself. No assertions-with-side-effects spotted in the sampled diffs. No new ingest/parse path found without adversarial-shaped coverage in the sampled set.

**🟡 Minor observations, not blocking:**
- Two commits (`929b82fc`, `3545f9fd`) are pure test-infrastructure fixes (mocking `previewBatchTarget`/secret-store deps to close flakes) rather than product fixes — fine, but worth noting they're not exercising new logic, just stabilizing existing suites.
- Coverage on the touched frontend files is uneven — `CheckNew.tsx` 76.66% lines, `ConnectionEdit.tsx` 76.92%, `Settings.tsx` 77.77%, `TriggersPanel`/`SuiteDrawer` in the high-70s/low-80s branch — all under the per-file 80% aspiration even though the all-src rollup clears the gate. None of these are newly-introduced-in-this-diff files at that low a number (they're existing files with partial coverage), so not a regression, but worth flagging for a follow-up coverage pass if there's appetite.
- `backend/app/services/dryrun_service.py` sits at 73% line coverage post-diff (33 missed lines) — it was touched by `d293399d` (SQL-echo stripping). Worth a closer look in a future pass since dry-run is exactly the kind of ingest-adjacent surface CONTRIBUTING flags, though the specific lines changed by this diff (the stripping call) are covered per the new `test_checks.py` assertions.

### 3. Cross-check against open issues

Checked all fix commits' issue references against `gh issue list --state open`. All issues explicitly deferred by this batch are filed and open as expected: `#1267` (observed_value's third shape, unparsed_value — deliberately out of scope), `#1266` (psycopg2-specific connect_args driver guard), `#1261` (centralize double-logged-traceback downgrade), `#1264`, `#1257`. None of these are regressions from this delta — they're intentionally-scoped-out follow-ups the batch itself filed. Nothing in the diff rediscovers a previously-known-and-still-open defect silently.

### Verdict

**Pass — all gates green, test quality acceptable. Ready to push / deploy.**

No hard findings. The `dryrun_service.py` coverage note and the handful of sub-80%-per-file frontend components are worth a `/gh-issue-from-finding` if you want to track them, but neither blocks this deploy — they're pre-existing gaps the diff didn't regress, and the batch's own discipline (mutation-checked assertions, real-object tests, deferred findings filed not dropped) is above the project's usual bar.</result>

import json
import os
import urllib.request
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, HTTPServer

ADDR = os.environ["OPENBAO_ADDR"]
MOUNT = os.environ["OPENBAO_MOUNT"]
TOKEN = os.environ["OPENBAO_TOKEN"]


class Handler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_GET(self):
        # path: /secret/<name>
        parts = self.path.strip("/").split("/")
        if len(parts) != 2 or parts[0] != "secret":
            self.send_response(404)
            self.end_headers()
            return
        name = parts[1]
        url = f"{ADDR}/v1/{MOUNT}/data/{name}"
        req = urllib.request.Request(url, headers={"X-Vault-Token": TOKEN})
        try:
            with urllib.request.urlopen(req) as resp:
                data = json.load(resp)

cd ~/Coding/Python/DataQ && gh issue create \
  --title "Decimal values in a failed range/threshold check crash result persistence, silently discarding the entire run" \
  --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Problem

Any Snowflake or Unity Catalog check that legitimately **fails** on a NUMERIC/DECIMAL column (price, quantity, subtotal, etc.) crashes the entire run during results persistence:

```
TypeError: Object of type Decimal is not JSON serializable
```

The crash happens in the JSONB bulk-insert of the `results` row (`backend/app/services/run_service.py`, `_run_suite`'s bulk insert). `backend/app/core/jsonsafe.py`'s `sanitize_json` (line ~24) explicitly coerces numpy scalars, pandas `NA`/`NaT`, dates, and non-finite floats — but has **no branch for `decimal.Decimal`**.

**Why it's easy to miss:** a *passing* check on a NUMERIC column never crashes — GX's failing-sample/observed-value payload only carries raw `Decimal` values when the check actually fails and rows are captured. So this only fires exactly when a warehouse check does its job and catches something real, and the entire run's results (not just that one check) are lost silently — no persisted row at all.

## Repro (verified live, Snowflake `RETAIL.ORDERS_HEADER`)

- `subtotal` (NUMERIC) range check, bound to guarantee 100% pass → succeeds, `n_results=1`.
- Same check, bound to guarantee 100% fail → crashes with the exact `Decimal` `TypeError`, reproduced twice independently.
- `channel` in-set FAIL (string column, not Decimal) → succeeds normally, confirming the bug is Decimal-specific, not FAIL-status-generic.

## Status: pre-existing, currently live in prod

Confirmed `backend/app/core/jsonsafe.py` at prod's deployed commit (`7018d772`) already lacks the `Decimal` branch — this predates the current release delta, it isn't a regression from recent work.

## Impact

Any Snowflake/UC suite with a range/threshold check on a currency, quantity, or other NUMERIC column that legitimately fails loses its entire run's results — the exact "the check caught something" case a DQ platform exists to preserve.

## Fix direction

Add a `decimal.Decimal` branch to `sanitize_json` (`backend/app/core/jsonsafe.py`), mirroring the existing numpy/pandas coercion pattern — e.g. `if isinstance(value, decimal.Decimal): return float(value)`.
EOF
)" \
  --label bug --milestone "v1.1 Week 6 — scale-aware execution + hardening + cycle close" 2>&1

1	"""Make values safe to persist into PostgreSQL ``JSONB`` columns.
2	
3	Great Expectations reports non-finite floats (``NaN``, ``Infinity``) inside
4	result payloads — e.g. a ``partial_unexpected_list`` of failing values, or an
5	``unexpected_percent`` on an empty batch. Python's ``json`` renders these as the
6	bare tokens ``NaN`` / ``Infinity``, which are not valid JSON and which Postgres
7	``JSONB`` rejects. ``sanitize_json`` walks a structure and replaces every
8	non-finite float with ``None`` — and coerces numpy scalars to native Python — so
9	GX results round-trip cleanly into the ``results`` table.
10	
11	Most GX 1.17 results are native Python scalars, but the pandas (flat-file / Unity
12	Catalog) execution engine returns **numpy** scalars in some payloads — notably the
13	``unexpected_index_list`` identifier rows (#415), whose ``numpy.int64`` values are
14	not JSON-serializable and would fail the JSONB insert. ``.item()`` coerces any numpy
15	scalar to its Python equivalent before the finite-float check.
16	"""
17	
18	from __future__ import annotations
19	
20	import math
21	from typing import Any
22	
23	
24	def sanitize_json(value: Any) -> Any:
25	    """Recursively coerce numpy scalars to native Python and replace non-finite
26	    floats with ``None``; leave the rest intact.
27	
28	    Containers are rebuilt (dicts/lists); tuples become lists so the result is
29	    JSON-native. Scalars other than numpy/non-finite-float pass through unchanged.
30	    """
31	    # A numpy scalar (int64/float64/bool_/…) — duck-typed by `item`+`dtype` so `core`
32	    # takes no numpy import (matching profile_service._to_native, and keeping the slim
33	    # typecheck env clean). `.item()` yields the Python equivalent; a numpy float then
34	    # flows into the finite check below.
35	    if hasattr(value, "item") and hasattr(value, "dtype"):
36	        value = value.item()
37	    # pandas' missing-value sentinels: Arrow-backed frames (the iceberg native read,
38	    # #716) surface null cells to GX payloads as `pd.NA` / `pd.NaT`, neither of which
39	    # is JSON-serializable (#751). Duck-typed by type name — same no-pandas-import
40	    # stance as the numpy branch above; both are singletons of these exact types.
41	    # MUST precede the isoformat branch: NaT has .isoformat() but must become null.
42	    if type(value).__name__ in ("NAType", "NaTType"):
43	        return None
44	    # Dates/datetimes: GX coerces between-style kwargs to `datetime.date` in
45	    # `expected_value`, and Arrow-backed frames yield `pd.Timestamp` sample values —
46	    # JSON has no native form for either. `.isoformat()` mirrors
47	    # profile_service._to_native (found live in the #751 review).
48	    if hasattr(value, "isoformat"):
49	        return value.isoformat()
50	    if isinstance(value, float):
51	        return value if math.isfinite(value) else None
52	    if isinstance(value, dict):
53	        return {key: sanitize_json(item) for key, item in value.items()}
54	    if isinstance(value, (list, tuple)):
55	        return [sanitize_json(item) for item in value]
56	    return value
57

"""Make values safe to persist into PostgreSQL ``JSONB`` columns.

Great Expectations reports non-finite floats (``NaN``, ``Infinity``) inside
result payloads — e.g. a ``partial_unexpected_list`` of failing values, or an
``unexpected_percent`` on an empty batch. Python's ``json`` renders these as the
bare tokens ``NaN`` / ``Infinity``, which are not valid JSON and which Postgres
``JSONB`` rejects. ``sanitize_json`` walks a structure and replaces every
non-finite float with ``None`` — and coerces numpy scalars to native Python — so
GX results round-trip cleanly into the ``results`` table.

Most GX 1.17 results are native Python scalars, but the pandas (flat-file / Unity
Catalog) execution engine returns **numpy** scalars in some payloads — notably the
``unexpected_index_list`` identifier rows (#415), whose ``numpy.int64`` values are
not JSON-serializable and would fail the JSONB insert. ``.item()`` coerces any numpy
scalar to its Python equivalent before the finite-float check.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import math

Fixed with a shared `_purge_column` helper reused across both columns. **#1230** (PII classifier evidence-window, option 2 chosen): the #1196 sample cap narrowed the classifier's evidence to 20 rows at capture time for pandas-backed datasources, which can flip a genuinely-PII column to "not PII" on a noisy 20-row window. Fixed by persisting a compact per-column `value_signal_summary` (5 small ints) over the FULL pre-cap population alongside the capped rows, which the classifier prefers when present and validates before trusting (rejects a summary with an inflated/inconsistent sub-count). A `/code-review` round live-verified a real crash — `_valid_summary`'s except clause didn't catch `OverflowError`, so a persisted JSONB summary with a huge float (`"n": 1e400` → `inf`) 500'd the entire read path instead of degrading to "no summary" — and found the summary wasn't threaded into the sibling `partial_unexpected_list`'s redaction (only `unexpected_index_list`'s), leaving a column masked on one list still shown on the other for the same run; both fixed and mutation-checked same-PR. **#1251** (consolidate hand-rolled `SecretStore` test doubles): five files each hand-rolled a near-identical class implementing the `SecretStore` Protocol, folded into one shared `backend/tests/support/fake_secret_store.py::FakeSecretStore`. The migration surfaced a real bug along the way — FastAPI's dependency-override resolution introspects the override CALLABLE's own signature, so a bare class (not a lambda) with constructor params, even all-defaulted ones, gets those params bound as request-level params and corrupts body validation for the endpoint under test; a bare `_WriteFailStore()` override was making `POST /connections` 422 instead of ever reaching the route. Three more were honesty-of-display: the panel picked the FIRST matching near-miss with `.find()`, so a second live mismatch on the same binding — two orchestrator connections reporting one DAG id against two different wrong envs, i.e. literally the #1186 ambiguity the feature exists to catch — was hidden behind the first; a failed near-miss fetch rendered identically to "no mismatch", so an outage read as healthy on the very screen built to surface it (the ADR-0039 lesson, in a new place); and the tooltip asserted the present tense ("runs keep landing in X … this binding has not fired and won't") for anything inside the 48h window while `updated_at` was fetched, typed, threaded through and never rendered — so a binding fixed an hour ago kept being told it was still broken. The last two were process: the tests drove the write LEAF rather than `orchestration_service._record_env_near_misses`, where the hashed tuple is actually *chosen*, so a change there could have desynced read from write and shipped green (a round-trip test through the real write path now covers it); and four new `assert client.get(...)` calls would have been deleted whole by `python -O` — caught by the #787 `test_assert_hygiene` guard, which is exactly what it is for. **CI caught one more that three green local runs did not**: splitting the near-miss resilience assertions into two `it`s failed the shared frontend run with `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'then')` AFTER all 92 files reported green — a late effect re-invoking the cleared mock. The file's own docstring had documented that exact hazard; the lesson recorded is to check the **exit code**, not the "N passed" line.))))))) |
